title: Mirar vs Ver: Look, See or Watch in Spanish?
seo_title: Mirar vs Ver: Look, See or Watch in Spanish?
meta_description: Mirar vs ver: when Spanish says look, see or watch. Clear rules, TV and movie usage, regional differences, useful expressions, common mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Look, see or watch? The difference is all about intention.

body_html:
Mirar vs ver maps onto English “look” and “see”, but with a twist: when it comes to watching TV or movies, Spanish usually says ver, not mirar. The core difference is intention. Ver is what reaches your eyes, whether you try or not; mirar is directing your eyes at something on purpose. Once you feel that difference, choosing the right verb becomes natural.

Quick answer
  • Ver = to see (perception) and usually to watch TV, movies and series.
  • Mirar = to look (at), to direct your eyes deliberately.
  • ¡Mira! means “Look!”; ¿Ves? means “See?”
  • In parts of South America, mirar la tele is also common.
{{toc}}

Mirar vs ver: the core rule

VerMirar
Meaningto see, perceive with the eyesto look, look at
IntentionNot necessaryDeliberate
ExampleNo veo nada sin lentes. I can’t see anything without glasses.Mira esa foto. Look at that photo.

The RAE dictionary defines mirar as directing your sight at something, while ver is perceiving it through sight. You can look (mirar) without seeing (ver): Miré por todas partes, pero no vi mis llaves. (I looked everywhere, but I didn’t see my keys.)

Watching TV, movies and series

Here English and Spanish part ways. For screens and shows, most Spanish speakers say ver:

  • Anoche vimos una película. Last night we watched a movie.
  • ¿Qué serie estás viendo? What series are you watching?
  • Me gusta ver el fútbol con amigos. I like watching soccer with friends.

In Argentina, Uruguay and some other countries, mirar la tele and mirar una película are also very common. Both are correct; ver is understood everywhere.

{{image:2}}

When to use mirar

  • Looking at something: Mira el cielo, está precioso. Look at the sky, it’s beautiful.
  • Getting attention: ¡Mira! Ahí está Pedro. Look! There’s Pedro.
  • Browsing in shops: Solo estoy mirando, gracias. I’m just looking, thanks.
  • Checking: Mira si hay leche en el refri. Check if there’s milk in the fridge.
  • Introducing an explanation: Mira, te explico. Look, let me explain.

That last use is extremely common in conversation: mira works like “look” or “listen” in English before an explanation.

When to use ver

  • Perception: ¿Ves ese edificio? Do you see that building?
  • Understanding: Ya veo. I see (I understand).
  • Meeting people: Nos vemos mañana. See you tomorrow.
  • Finding out: Vamos a ver qué pasa. Let’s see what happens.
  • Visiting: Fui a ver a mi abuela. I went to see my grandmother.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Conjugation note

Mirar is regular. Ver is irregular in places: present veo, ves, ve, vemos, veis, ven; past vi, viste, vio (no accents); past participle visto; imperfect veía.

Real conversations

At home

  • A: ¿Qué quieres ver esta noche? (What do you want to watch tonight?)
  • B: Mira, hay una serie nueva en Netflix. ¿La vemos? (Look, there’s a new series on Netflix. Shall we watch it?)

In a shop

  • Assistant: ¿Le puedo ayudar en algo? (Can I help you with anything?)
  • You: No, gracias, solo estoy mirando. (No, thanks, I’m just looking.)

Looking for something

  • A: ¿Has visto mi celular? (Have you seen my phone?)
  • B: No. ¿Has mirado en el carro? (No. Have you looked in the car?)

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Miré una película anoche.Vi una película anoche.Ver is the default for movies (except in some regions)
Estoy viendo, gracias. (in a shop)Estoy mirando, gracias.Browsing is deliberate looking
Mira a la foto.Mira la foto.No a before things (only before people)
Ví / vióvi / vioThese forms have no accent
{{image:3}}

Useful expressions

  • A ver… Let’s see… (very common filler)
  • ¿Viste? See? / You know? (Argentina and Uruguay)
  • No tener nada que ver: to have nothing to do with. Eso no tiene nada que ver.
  • Mirar mal a alguien: to give someone a dirty look.
  • Ver venir algo: to see something coming.

Mirar vs ver has a twin pair for hearing: {{link:oir-vs-escuchar|oír vs escuchar}} works in exactly the same way, with perception versus intention. For the full set, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

One more useful contrast: Mírame (Look at me) asks for attention, while ¿Me ves? (Can you see me?) checks perception, for example on a video call with a bad connection.

Try it yourself

Translate these sentences, then check your answers:

  1. Look at this! (¡Mira esto!)
  2. We watched the match at a bar. (Vimos el partido en un bar.)
  3. I see what you mean. (Ya veo lo que quieres decir.)
  4. She looked out of the window but saw nobody. (Miró por la ventana, pero no vio a nadie.)
  5. See you on Monday! (¡Nos vemos el lunes!)

Sentence four contains both verbs: the deliberate looking and the result, or lack of it.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Use mirar when you point your eyes on purpose, and ver for what you perceive, understand or watch on a screen. And when in doubt about a movie or series, ver is the safe choice everywhere.

faq.q: What is the difference between mirar and ver?
faq.a: Ver means to see or perceive with your eyes and is also the usual verb for watching TV and movies. Mirar means to look at something deliberately.

faq.q: Do you say ver la tele or mirar la tele?
faq.a: Ver la tele is the most common and understood everywhere. Mirar la tele is also common in Argentina, Uruguay and some other countries.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m just looking” in a shop?
